info.text: Let's use looping audio tracks to create an experimental musical instrument for making ambient generative soundscapes!
info.title: Getting Started
Adding CSS
info.text: Before we get started, I'm just going to add a bit of (optional) CSS to make things look nice...

info.title: Adding an Audio File
info.text: For version 1, we'll start simple by adding just a single audio file...

info.title: The Audio Tag
info.text:
Let's create an <audio> tag.
Inside the opening tag, we'll add two attributes:

  • src, which is the URL to your audio file, and
  • controls, which displays the browser's built-in play/pause/volume controls on the page.

info.title: Multiple Files and Looping
info.text: We're off to a good start. Now in Version 2, we'll add multiple audio tracks, and make them loop.

info.title: Adding More Elements
info.text: ...and add two more! (in this demo the files are the same, but you can use any sources you'd like)

info.title: The Loop Attribute
info.text:
By default, your <audio> files will stop playing once they reach the end.

Let's fix this by adding a loop attribute to our 3 files.

info.title: Looping Forever
info.text: Now the audio elements will loop forever once they get to the end.

info.title: A Phasing Effect
info.text: The looping elements will phase in and out of one another, creating an evolving, generative soundscape!

info.title: You Built an Instrument!
info.text: And just like that, you've created an experimental audio controller! Congrats!

info.title: Outro
info.text: You're following in the footsteps of sound artists like Steve Reich, William Basinski, and Terry Riley (+ many others) who used looping and phasing to create ambient soundscapes.

info.title: Next Steps
info.text:
Feel free to pause this demo to play around with the looping audio by pressing the [done] button.

When you're ready to continue, head over to Part 2, where we'll give each track a unique ID and wire up a "Play All" button.
